e-10897.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
e-10897.problem: Simplify the integral $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx$ using symmetry.
e-10897.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .
$$

Notice that $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function, we have

$$
\int_{-2}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.
$$

e-10898.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
e-10898.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

- $\displaystyle \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 (e^x+e^{-x}) \, \textrm dx$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\pi}^{2\pi} \sin(2x) \, \textrm dx$
e-10898.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x) = 4x^3$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =4(-x)^{3} \\  & =-4{x}^{3} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
\int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

- The function $g(x) = e^x+e^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & ={e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & ={e}^{-x}+{e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}+{e}^{-x} \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x) = \sin(2x)$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form $\displaystyle \int_{-a}^a h(x)\,\textrm d x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. So, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

e-10911.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
e-10911.problem: Given that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,$ what is the value of $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x  \, \textrm dx?$
e-10911.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Notice that $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
\int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x  \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{6})$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡((-x)^{6}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{6}) \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{6})$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{6})\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{6})\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5(-x)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-5x) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x) \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.

$$

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=3\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{4})$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡((-x)^{4}) \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{4}) \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=3\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{4})$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}3\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{1}3\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{2}-3$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =((-x)^{2}-3) \\  & =({x}^{2}-3) \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=({x}^{2}-3)$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-9}^{9}({x}^{2}-3)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{9}({x}^{2}-3)\,\text{d}x.
$$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $h(x)={x}^{3}-2$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{3}-2 \\  & =-{x}^{3}-2 \\  & =-({x}^{3}+2) \\  & \ne -h(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{5}+(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{5}-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-({x}^{5}+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{5}+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{(-x)^{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}}) \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
